items.stem: Which of the following best describes "natural rights"?
options: Rights recognised and protected by a specific legal system, such as rights in a national constitution or a treaty
Rights believed to exist independently of law or government, derived from human nature or reason, such as Locke's life, liberty and property
The UDHR together with the ICCPR and ICESCR (1966) and their optional protocols
The UN body (1946–2006) that drafted the UDHR, chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, later replaced by the Human Rights Council
items.answer: Rights believed to exist independently of law or government, derived from human nature or reason, such as Locke's life, liberty and property
items.markingKey: B. "natural rights" is rights believed to exist independently of law or government, derived from human nature or reason, such as Locke's life, liberty and property.

items.stem: Distinguish between natural rights and legal rights.
items.answer: Natural rights are held to exist by virtue of being human, independent of law; legal rights exist because a legal system recognises and enforces them and can be changed by legislation.
items.markingKey: Natural rights are held to exist by virtue of being human, independent of law; legal rights exist because a legal system recognises and enforces them and can be changed by legislation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that human rights only exist if a country's government has written them into law. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: This confuses legal rights with human rights; human rights are claimed to belong to everyone, and international law (UDHR, treaties) recognises them even where national law does not.
items.markingKey: This confuses legal rights with human rights; human rights are claimed to belong to everyone, and international law (UDHR, treaties) recognises them even where national law does not. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Classify each right as natural, legal or moral (choose the best fit) and justify: (a) a right to vote at 16 in Austria, (b) the right not to be tortured, (c) a claim that future generations have a right to a liveable climate.
items.answer: (a) legal – created by Austrian law (2007); (b) widely seen as natural/human right, also legal under the Convention against Torture; (c) moral – argued ethically, only partly recognised in law (e.g. some court cases). 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: (a) legal – created by Austrian law (2007); (b) widely seen as natural/human right, also legal under the Convention against Torture; (c) moral – argued ethically, only partly recognised in law (e.g. some court cases). 1 mark each.

items.stem: A student claims that rights and justice mean exactly the same thing. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Rights are entitlements of individuals or groups; justice is a broader principle of fairness about how a society treats and distributes among its members.
items.markingKey: Rights are entitlements of individuals or groups; justice is a broader principle of fairness about how a society treats and distributes among its members. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Rights are not gifts from governments. Governments are created to secure them, and when they fail, the people may change them."
— Paraphrase of the US Declaration of Independence (1776)

With reference to the source, explain the idea of natural rights.
items.answer: Rights exist before government and are not granted by it; government's legitimacy depends on protecting them – Locke's natural rights theory.
items.markingKey: Rights exist before government and are not granted by it; government's legitimacy depends on protecting them – Locke's natural rights theory. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Basic rights and freedoms to which all people are entitled simply because they are human, regardless of nationality, sex, ethnicity or other status"?
options: legal rights
human rights
inalienable
moral rights
items.answer: human rights
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of human rights.

items.stem: "Rights and justice mean exactly the same thing." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Rights are entitlements of individuals or groups; justice is a broader principle of fairness about how a society treats and distributes among its members.
items.markingKey: Rights are entitlements of individuals or groups; justice is a broader principle of fairness about how a society treats and distributes among its members. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A protester says: "The law says I cannot criticise the king, but I have a right to speak freely." Identify the two types of rights in conflict and explain.
items.answer: Legal restriction (lèse-majesté law, e.g. in Thailand) vs natural/moral/human right to freedom of expression (UDHR Art. 19); the protester appeals to a right above national law.
items.markingKey: Legal restriction (lèse-majesté law, e.g. in Thailand) vs natural/moral/human right to freedom of expression (UDHR Art. 19); the protester appeals to a right above national law.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"A right without a remedy is no right at all. Unless a court can enforce it, a right is only a hope."
— Legal commentary, 2018 (adapted)

Identify the view of rights in the source and explain one criticism of it.
items.answer: A legal positivist view – rights only exist meaningfully when enforceable by law. Criticism: moral and human rights can exist and motivate change before courts recognise them (e.g. abolition, civil rights).
items.markingKey: A legal positivist view – rights only exist meaningfully when enforceable by law. Criticism: moral and human rights can exist and motivate change before courts recognise them (e.g. abolition, civil rights). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Discuss the extent to which the concept of natural rights remains useful in contemporary global politics.
items.answer: Discuss foundations (Locke, UDHR "inherent dignity"), criticisms (Bentham, cultural relativism), and contemporary use (civil disobedience, climate litigation, refugee claims). Reach a judgement.
items.markingKey: Discuss foundations (Locke, UDHR "inherent dignity"), criticisms (Bentham, cultural relativism), and contemporary use (civil disobedience, climate litigation, refugee claims). Reach a judgement.

items.stem: Which of the following is a second-generation right?
options: The right to development
The right to a fair trial
Freedom of assembly
The right to education
items.answer: The right to education
items.markingKey: D. Education is an economic, social and cultural right (ICESCR Art. 13).

items.stem: Kwame writes: "Third-generation rights are legally binding in the same way as first-generation rights." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Most third-generation rights are in declarations or emerging law and are less enforceable; though regional instruments such as the African Charter (1981) include peoples' rights.
items.markingKey: Most third-generation rights are in declarations or emerging law and are less enforceable; though regional instruments such as the African Charter (1981) include peoples' rights. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between civil and political rights and economic, social and cultural rights.
items.answer: Civil and political rights protect freedom from state interference and participation (speech, trial, vote) and are immediately applicable; economic, social and cultural rights require provision (health, education, housing) and are realised progressively according to resources.
items.markingKey: Civil and political rights protect freedom from state interference and participation (speech, trial, vote) and are immediately applicable; economic, social and cultural rights require provision (health, education, housing) and are realised progressively according to resources. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that economic and social rights are not real human rights because they cost money. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: All rights cost money – fair trials need courts and elections need administration; the ICESCR makes socio-economic rights legally binding on 170+ states parties, subject to progressive realisation.
items.markingKey: All rights cost money – fair trials need courts and elections need administration; the ICESCR makes socio-economic rights legally binding on 170+ states parties, subject to progressive realisation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A government says it cannot afford universal primary health care. Explain how the principle of progressive realisation applies.
items.answer: Under ICESCR Art. 2(1), the state must take deliberate steps to the maximum of available resources, avoid retrogression and prioritise minimum core obligations (essential primary care); lack of resources does not remove the obligation.
items.markingKey: Under ICESCR Art. 2(1), the state must take deliberate steps to the maximum of available resources, avoid retrogression and prioritise minimum core obligations (essential primary care); lack of resources does not remove the obligation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Inter-American Court and Indigenous land rights (Awas Tingni v Nicaragua, 2001) shows collective rights.
items.answer: The court ruled that Nicaragua violated the Mayagna community's right to property by granting logging concessions on their land. a regional court recognised a group's communal right to land, extending property rights to collective form
items.markingKey: Context (The court ruled that Nicaragua violated the Mayagna community's right to property by granting logging concessions on their land.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a regional court recognised a group's communal right to land, extending property rights to collective form – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to collective rights.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Third-generation rights weaken the concept of human rights."
items.answer: They broaden human rights to global challenges, but their weak enforceability means they complement rather than replace core rights.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: vague and hard to enforce; unclear who holds the duty; dilute core rights. Arguments against: address real global problems (climate, development); reflect Global South priorities; build on solidarity. Supported judgement: They broaden human rights to global challenges, but their weak enforceability means they complement rather than replace core rights.

items.stem: Analyse how one contemporary issue involves rights from more than one generation.
items.answer: E.g. climate change: right to life (first), health and food (second), healthy environment and development (third); Indigenous land conflicts; digital rights. Show interdependence and tensions.
items.markingKey: E.g. climate change: right to life (first), health and food (second), healthy environment and development (third); Indigenous land conflicts; digital rights. Show interdependence and tensions.

items.stem: Briefly explain why some critics argue that the "generations" model is misleading.
items.answer: It implies a hierarchy and a sequence, but rights are indivisible and interdependent (Vienna 1993): e.g. the right to vote means little without education, and many socio-economic rights were demanded alongside civil rights.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It implies a hierarchy and a sequence, but rights are indivisible and interdependent (Vienna 1993): e.g. the right to vote means little without education, and many socio-economic rights were demanded alongside civil rights. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why collective rights can conflict with individual rights.
items.answer: A group's right to preserve its culture may justify practices that limit individuals' choices – e.g. community control over land or customary rules about membership and gender roles.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A group's right to preserve its culture may justify practices that limit individuals' choices – e.g. community control over land or customary rules about membership and gender roles. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why second-generation rights were historically associated with socialist states.
items.answer: During the Cold War, the Soviet bloc emphasised economic and social rights (work, housing, health) as essential, while Western states emphasised civil and political rights; this is one reason the UDHR rights were split into two covenants in 1966.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: During the Cold War, the Soviet bloc emphasised economic and social rights (work, housing, health) as essential, while Western states emphasised civil and political rights; this is one reason the UDHR rights were split into two covenants in 1966. items.stem:
Read the source below.

"We do not ask for charity. We ask for the right to our land, our language and our way of life as a people."
— Statement by an Indigenous leader at the UN Permanent Forum, 2019 (adapted)

Identify the type of rights claimed in the source and explain it.
items.answer: Collective (third-generation / group) rights – rights held by a people to land, language and culture, recognised in UNDRIP (2007).
items.markingKey: Collective (third-generation / group) rights – rights held by a people to land, language and culture, recognised in UNDRIP (2007). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that civil and political rights are more important than economic and social rights?
items.answer: The two sets of rights are interdependent; prioritising one undermines the other, so ranking them is misleading.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: protect against tyranny; enable people to demand other rights; immediately enforceable. Arguments against: survival needs come first (Sen, capabilities); indivisibility (Vienna 1993); hunger undermines freedom. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "International Bill of Human Rights"?

Rights recognised and protected by a specific legal system, such as rights in a national constitution or a treaty
The principle that all human rights are equally important and interdependent, affirmed in the 1993 Vienna Declaration
The UDHR together with the ICCPR and ICESCR (1966) and their optional protocols
items.answer: The UDHR together with the ICCPR and ICESCR (1966) and their optional protocols

items.stem: Distinguish between a convention and a declaration.
items.answer: A declaration states principles and commitments but is not legally binding by itself; a convention (treaty) is legally binding on states that ratify it.

items.stem: A student claims that the UDHR was signed and ratified as a treaty by all UN member states in 1948. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It was adopted by a General Assembly vote (48–0–8) by the then 58 members (two absent); declarations are not ratified.
items.markingKey: It was adopted by a General Assembly vote (48–0–8) by the then 58 members (two absent); declarations are not ratified. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the UDHR and decolonisation shows the evolution of human rights after 1948.
items.answer: Newly independent states such as Ghana and India drew on UDHR principles; the 1960 Declaration on Granting Independence to Colonial Countries (Res. 1514) linked self-determination to human rights. anti-colonial movements used human rights language to challenge empire, extending universal rights to colonised peoples
items.markingKey: Context (Newly independent states such as Ghana and India drew on UDHR principles; the 1960 Declaration on Granting Independence to Colonial Countries (Res. 1514) linked self-determination to human rights.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Identify which UDHR article is most relevant to each situation: (a) a journalist jailed for criticising the government, (b) a person detained without trial, (c) a refugee fleeing persecution.
items.answer: (a) Art. 19 – freedom of opinion and expression; (b) Art. 9 – no arbitrary arrest/detention (also Art. 10 fair hearing); (c) Art. 14 – right to seek asylum. 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: (a) Art. 19 – freedom of opinion and expression; (b) Art. 9 – no arbitrary arrest/detention (also Art. 10 fair hearing); (c) Art. 14 – right to seek asylum. 1 mark each.

items.stem: Analyse how the historical context of 1945–1948 shaped the content of the UDHR.
items.answer: Discuss WWII and Holocaust (life, dignity, prohibition of torture), Cold War compromise (both civil and socio-economic rights), sovereignty concerns (non-binding), colonial context (limited representation; later decolonisation). Evaluate the legacy.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Human Rights Day"?

The UDHR together with the ICCPR and ICESCR (1966) and their optional protocols
10 December, the anniversary of the adoption of the UDHR in 1948
Describing rights that cannot be given up, sold or taken away

items.stem: Tomás writes: "The UDHR was written only by Western drafters." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The drafting committee included Peng Chun Chang (China), Charles Malik (Lebanon), Hansa Mehta (India) and others; Mehta is credited with changing "all men" to "all human beings" in Article 1.

items.stem: Outline two features of the post-1945 international context that explain why the UDHR was adopted in 1948.
items.answer: The shock of WWII and the Holocaust; the creation of the UN with a Charter referring to human rights (Art. 1(3)); the onset of the Cold War requiring compromise; emerging decolonisation. 2 marks each.

items.stem: Which of the following is the best example of a legal right that is not universally accepted as a moral right?

The right not to be tortured
A right to carry firearms under the US Second Amendment
The right to life
items.answer: A right to carry firearms under the US Second Amendment

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "progressive realisation".
items.answer: The principle that states must take steps, to the maximum of available resources, to achieve economic, social and cultural rights over time (ICESCR Art. 2)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the principle that states must take steps, to the maximum of available resources, to achieve economic, social and cultural rights over time (ICESCR Art. 2). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Rights grounded in ethical principles that people ought to have, whether or not the law recognises them"?
options: indivisibility of rights
progressive realisation
moral rights
International Bill of Human Rights
items.answer: moral rights
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of moral rights.

items.stem: Define the term "International Bill of Human Rights".
items.answer: The UDHR together with the ICCPR and ICESCR (1966) and their optional protocols
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the UDHR together with the ICCPR and ICESCR (1966) and their optional protocols. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between individual rights and collective rights.
items.answer: Individual rights are held by each person (e.g. freedom of religion); collective rights are held by groups as such (e.g. a people's right to self-determination or Indigenous land rights).
items.markingKey: Individual rights are held by each person (e.g. freedom of religion); collective rights are held by groups as such (e.g. a people's right to self-determination or Indigenous land rights). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between natural rights and legal rights.
items.answer: Natural rights are held to exist by virtue of being human, independent of law; legal rights exist because a legal system recognises and enforces them and can be changed by legislation.
items.markingKey: Natural rights are held to exist by virtue of being human, independent of law; legal rights exist because a legal system recognises and enforces them and can be changed by legislation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the UDHR and the ICCPR.
items.answer: The UDHR (1948) is a non-binding General Assembly declaration covering all categories of rights; the ICCPR (1966, in force 1976) is a binding treaty for its states parties covering civil and political rights, monitored by the Human Rights Committee.
items.markingKey: The UDHR (1948) is a non-binding General Assembly declaration covering all categories of rights; the ICCPR (1966, in force 1976) is a binding treaty for its states parties covering civil and political rights, monitored by the Human Rights Committee. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why rights and justice are closely connected.
items.answer: Rights set out what individuals are owed; justice concerns whether a society gives people what they are owed and distributes benefits and burdens fairly, so violations of rights are injustices.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Rights set out what individuals are owed; justice concerns whether a society gives people what they are owed and distributes benefits and burdens fairly, so violations of rights are injustices. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why some states abstained in the 1948 vote on the UDHR.
items.answer: The Soviet bloc objected that it emphasised civil liberties over socio-economic rights and state sovereignty; South Africa objected to equality provisions that challenged apartheid; Saudi Arabia objected to freedom to change religion and equal marriage rights.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The Soviet bloc objected that it emphasised civil liberties over socio-economic rights and state sovereignty; South Africa objected to equality provisions that challenged apartheid; Saudi Arabia objected to freedom to change religion and equal marriage rights. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using UNGA recognition of the right to a healthy environment (2022) as an example, explain the emergence of third-generation rights.
items.answer: In July 2022 the General Assembly voted 161–0 with 8 abstentions to recognise the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment. states recognised a new solidarity right, though it is not yet a binding treaty obligation
items.markingKey: Context (In July 2022 the General Assembly voted 161–0 with 8 abstentions to recognise the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Using the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in apartheid South Africa as an example, explain rights as a basis for justice claims.
items.answer: The apartheid state denied black South Africans voting and movement rights; the ANC's 1955 Freedom Charter claimed equal rights for all. movements appealed to universal rights to expose the injustice of a legal order and build international pressure
items.markingKey: Context (The apartheid state denied black South Africans voting and movement rights; the ANC's 1955 Freedom Charter claimed equal rights for all.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: movements appealed to universal rights to expose the injustice of a legal order and build international pressure – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to rights as a basis for justice claims.

items.stem: "The UDHR was signed and ratified as a treaty by all UN member states in 1948." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It was adopted by a General Assembly vote (48–0–8) by the then 58 members (two absent); declarations are not ratified.
items.markingKey: It was adopted by a General Assembly vote (48–0–8) by the then 58 members (two absent); declarations are not ratified. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which South Africa's Grootboom case (2000) shows the justiciability of socio-economic rights.
items.answer: The Constitutional Court held that the state's housing programme was unreasonable because it made no provision for people in desperate need, enforcing the constitutional right to access to housing. a court enforced a second-generation right, showing such rights can be legally meaningful
items.markingKey: Context (The Constitutional Court held that the state's housing programme was unreasonable because it made no provision for people in desperate need, enforcing the constitutional right to access to housing.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Outline one way in which the 2017 Indian Supreme Court privacy ruling (Puttaswamy) shows how legal rights are recognised.
items.answer: A nine-judge bench unanimously held that privacy is a fundamental right under the Indian Constitution. the court turned a moral claim to privacy into an enforceable constitutional right
items.markingKey: Context (A nine-judge bench unanimously held that privacy is a fundamental right under the Indian Constitution.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the court turned a moral claim to privacy into an enforceable constitutional right – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how legal rights are recognised.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Nuremberg trials (1945–1946) shows the historical context of the UDHR.
items.answer: Leading Nazi officials were tried for crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity by an international military tribunal. Nuremberg established that individuals, including state officials, can be held accountable for atrocities, a principle that shaped the post-war human rights order

items.stem: "Economic and social rights are not real human rights because they cost money." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: All rights cost money – fair trials need courts and elections need administration; the ICESCR makes socio-economic rights legally binding on 170+ states parties, subject to progressive realisation.
items.markingKey: All rights cost money – fair trials need courts and elections need administration; the ICESCR makes socio-economic rights legally binding on 170+ states parties, subject to progressive realisation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Rights are meaningless without effective enforcement."
items.answer: Enforcement makes rights effective, but rights also have normative and mobilising power even when weakly enforced.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: violations go unpunished (Syria, Myanmar); rights depend on courts. items.stem: To what extent is it true that the UDHR has been the most important development in the history of human rights?
items.answer: The UDHR is foundational, but its importance lies in what it inspired; binding treaties and enforcement mechanisms made rights effective.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: foundational for all later treaties; universal reach; cited in national constitutions. Arguments against: non-binding; binding covenants and courts (ICC, ECtHR) arguably more important; abolition of slavery and decolonisation earlier or parallel. items.stem: Evaluate the claim that third-generation rights weaken the concept of human rights.
items.answer: They broaden human rights to global challenges, but their weak enforceability means they complement rather than replace core rights.
